claim: LPL undergoes spontaneous inactivation via global unfolding.
source: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) undergoes spontaneous inactivation via global unfolding and this unfolding is prevented by GPIHBP1 (Mysling et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mysling et al., 2016

claim: GPIHBP1 prevents spontaneous unfolding of LPL.
source: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) undergoes spontaneous inactivation via global unfolding and this unfolding is prevented by GPIHBP1 (Mysling et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mysling et al., 2016

claim: ANGPTL4 inactivates LPL by catalyzing the unfolding of its hydrolase domain.
source: We now show: (1) that ANGPTL4 inactivates LPL by catalyzing the unfolding of its hydrolase domain
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS experimental data showing time- and dose-dependent unfolding of LPL's hydrolase domain in the presence of ANGPTL4

claim: Binding to GPIHBP1 renders LPL largely refractory to ANGPTL4 inhibition.
source: (2) that binding to GPIHBP1 renders LPL largely refractory to this inhibition
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced LPL unfolding in the presence of GPIHBP1 and ANGPTL4

claim: Both the LU domain and the intrinsically disordered acidic domain of GPIHBP1 are required for protection of LPL from ANGPTL4.
source: (3) that both the LU domain and the intrinsically disordered acidic domain of GPIHBP1 are required for this protective effect
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing full-length GPIHBP1 with truncated versions

claim: A common polymorphic variant in ANGPTL4 (E15K) results in lower plasma triglyceride levels.
source: Genetic studies have found that a common polymorphic variant in ANGPTL4 results in lower plasma triglyceride levels.
evidence: Supported by reference to genetic studies

claim: The ANGPTL4 E15K variant is less efficient in catalyzing the unfolding of LPL.
source: (1) that this ANGPTL4 variant is less efficient in catalyzing the unfolding of LPL
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data showing reduced unfolding efficacy of ANGPTL4 E15K compared to wild-type

claim: The Glu-to-Lys substitution in ANGPTL4 E15K destabilizes its N-terminal α-helix.
source: (2) that its Glu-to-Lys substitution destabilizes its N-terminal α-helix
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data showing increased deuterium uptake in the N-terminal α-helix region of ANGPTL4 E15K

claim: LPL is secreted into the interstitial spaces by myocytes and adipocytes.
source: LPL is secreted into the interstitial spaces by myocytes and adipocytes but is then shuttled to the capillary lumen by an endothelial transporter, glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored high density lipoprotein–binding protein 1 (GPIHBP1) (Fong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fong et al., 2016

claim: GPIHBP1 shuttles LPL to the capillary lumen.
source: LPL is secreted into the interstitial spaces by myocytes and adipocytes but is then shuttled to the capillary lumen by an endothelial transporter, glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored high density lipoprotein–binding protein 1 (GPIHBP1) (Fong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fong et al., 2016

claim: GPIHBP1 is required for the margination of TRLs along capillaries.
source: This endothelial cell LPL transporter is also required for the margination of TRLs along capillaries (Goulbourne et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goulbourne et al., 2014

claim: Genetic ablation of GPIHBP1 in mice leads to sustained elevations in plasma triglyceride levels.
source: Disruption of LPL transport by either genetic ablation of GPIHBP1 in mice (Beigneux et al., 2007) or by loss-of-function missense mutations in humans leads to sustained elevations in plasma triglyceride levels—a condition known as familial chylomicronemia (Ariza et al., 2016; Beigneux et al., 2015, 2009b; Olivecrona et al., 2010; Plengpanich et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Loss-of-function missense mutations in GPIHBP1 in humans lead to familial chylomicronemia.
source: Disruption of LPL transport by either genetic ablation of GPIHBP1 in mice (Beigneux et al., 2007) or by loss-of-function missense mutations in humans leads to sustained elevations in plasma triglyceride levels—a condition known as familial chylomicronemia (Ariza et al., 2016; Beigneux et al., 2015, 2009b; Olivecrona et al., 2010; Plengpanich et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: LPL activity is regulated by endogenous protein inhibitors ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4, and ANGPTL8.
source: Appropriate distribution of lipid nutrients to tissues is, however, not only controlled by the availability of LPL and GPIHBP1, but is also tightly regulated by endogenous protein inhibitors of LPL activity (angiopoietin-like (ANGPTL) proteins 3, 4, and 8).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: Reciprocal regulation of ANGPTL4 expression in brown and white adipocytes with prolonged cold exposure results in high LPL activity in brown adipocytes.
source: Reciprocal regulation of ANGPTL4 expression in brown and white adipocytes with prolonged cold exposure results in high LPL activity in brown adipocytes and ensures the delivery of lipid nutrients for adaptive thermogenesis (Dijk et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dijk et al., 2015

claim: Pharmacological inhibition or genetic ablation of ANGPTL3 or ANGPTL4 results in lower plasma triglyceride levels.
source: The relevance of these inhibitors to LPL-mediated TRL processing in vivo is illustrated by lower plasma triglyceride levels with pharmacological inhibition or genetic ablation of ANGPTL3 or ANGPTL4 (Desai et al., 2007; Gusarova et al., 2015; Köster et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The ANGPTL4 E40K polymorphic variant is associated with mild hypotriglyceridemia and reduced risk of coronary artery disease.
source: Additional evidence for their physiological importance are provided by genome-wide association studies (GWAS), which showed that a polymorphic variant of ANGPTL4, E40K (E15K in the mature protein) is associated with mild hypotriglyceridemia and reduced risk of coronary artery disease (Dewey et al., 2016; Helgadottir et al., 2016; Stitziel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to GWAS studies

claim: The N-terminal coiled-coil domain of ANGPTL4 catalyzes the conversion of LPL homodimers to inactive LPL monomers.
source: An early report suggested that the N-terminal coiled-coil domain of ANGPTL4 catalyzed the conversion of LPL homodimers to inactive LPL monomers (Sukonina et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sukonina et al., 2006

claim: ANGPTL4 inhibits LPL by a reversible and noncompetitive mechanism.
source: However, this conclusion has been challenged by a report suggesting that ANGPTL4 inhibits LPL by a reversible and noncompetitive mechanism (Lafferty et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lafferty et al., 2013

claim: LPL irreversibly loses catalytic activity by undergoing a time- and temperature-dependent global unfolding of its serine hydrolase domain.
source: We previously showed that LPL irreversibly loses catalytic activity by undergoing a time- and temperature-dependent global unfolding of its serine hydrolase domain (Mysling et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mysling et al., 2016

claim: The C-terminal lipid-binding domain of LPL remains stably folded during spontaneous inactivation.
source: In contrast, the C-terminal lipid-binding domain of LPL remains stably folded.
evidence: Supported by previous experimental data from Mysling et al., 2016

claim: 10 µM LPL undergoes a slow spontaneous transition into an unfolded state with 29% of the LPL being unfolded after 30 min at 25°C.
source: Mass spectrometry revealed that 10 µM LPL undergoes a slow spontaneous transition into an unfolded state during the selected incubation time interval (0–30 min), with 29% of the LPL being unfolded after 30 min at 25°C (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1

claim: 7.0 ± 0.7% of LPL was in the unfolded state after 5 min of spontaneous unfolding.
source: Quantitative assessment of this distribution reveals that 7.0 ± 0.7% of LPL was in the unfolded state after 5 min.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of mass spectrometry data

claim: Adding 1 µM ANGPTL41–159 to 10 µM LPL greatly accelerated the rate of LPL unfolding, with 60.3 ± 2.3% of the LPL being unfolded after 5 min.
source: Adding 1 µM ANGPTL41–159 to 10 µM LPL greatly accelerated the rate of LPL unfolding, with 60.3 ± 2.3% of the LPL being unfolded after 5 min (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Substoichiometric amounts of ANGPTL4 (molar ratio of 1:10) unfold >50% of LPL molecules in 5 min.
source: Even though the amount of ANGPTL41–159 added was substoichiometric relative to LPL (a molar ratio of 1:10), ANGPTL4 was responsible for unfolding >50% of LPL molecules in 5 min.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent unfolding

claim: The unfolding of >50% of LPL molecules by substoichiometric amounts of ANGPTL4 constitutes a strong argument in favor of the catalytic nature of ANGPTL4-mediated LPL inactivation.
source: This noticeable amount of LPL unfolding by substoichiometric amounts of ANGPTL4 constitutes a strong argument in favor of the catalytic nature of ANGPTL4-mediated LPL inactivation (Sukonina et al., 2006).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and citation to Sukonina et al., 2006

claim: Lower amounts of ANGPTL4 (0.5 µM, 0.25 µM) provide dose-dependent inactivation of LPL.
source: Those studies provided clear evidence for a dose-dependent inactivation of LPL by ANGPTL4 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: 0.25 µM ANGPTL4 (molar ratio of 1:40 relative to LPL) resulted in 74 ± 6% LPL unfolding after 30 min compared to 28.6 ± 1.3% spontaneous unfolding.
source: The lowest ANGPTL4 concentration tested resulted in 74 ± 6% LPL unfolding after 30 min compared to a spontaneous unfolding of 28.6 ± 1.3% in the buffer lacking ANGPTL4.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The unfolding efficacy of ANGPTL41–159 is 1.6 ± 0.2 molecules of LPL per ANGPTL4 molecule per min at 25°C.
source: From early time point measurements, where substrate depletion was negligible, we estimate that the unfolding efficacy of our ANGPTL41–159 preparation was 1.6 ± 0.2 molecules of LPL per ANGPTL4 molecule per min at 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: ANGPTL41–159 causes time- and dose-dependent inhibition of LPL catalytic activity measured with [3H]triolein.
source: When identical incubations of LPL and ANGPTL4 were analyzed for lipolytic activity with [3H]triolein, we found a similar time- and dose-dependent inhibition of LPL catalytic activity by ANGPTL41–159 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Spontaneous and ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding of LPL result in similar conformational changes.
source: In comparing the deuterium uptake across all LPL peptides, we observed no differences in the pattern of deuterium uptake into LPL molecules undergoing spontaneous or ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1C

claim: All peptides showing bimodality during LPL unfolding are confined to the serine hydrolase domain of LPL.
source: Of note, all peptides showing bimodality were confined to the serine hydrolase domain of LPL (Figure 1E); none were in the C-terminal lipid-binding domain.
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Different means of LPL inactivation are mirrored by similar conformational endpoints whether they occur spontaneously or are catalyzed by ANGPTL4.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that different means of LPL inactivation are mirrored by similar conformational endpoints whether they occur spontaneously or are catalyzed by ANGPTL4.
evidence: Inference based on HDX-MS data comparing spontaneous and ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding

claim: ANGPTL4 is prone to various degrees of oligomerization via intermolecular disulfide bonds involving Cys51 and Cys55.
source: Several reports show that ANGPTL4 is prone to various degrees of oligomerization via intermolecular disulfide bonds involving Cys51 and Cys55 in ANGPTL4´s N-terminal coiled-coil domain (Ge et al., 2004a, 2004b; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The ANGPTL41–159 preparation contains disulfide-linked oligomers, predominantly in the form of dimers comprising no more than 10% of the protein preparation.
source: Our ANGPTL41–159 preparation also contained disulfide-linked oligomers, although they were predominantly in the form of dimers and comprised no more than 10% of the protein preparation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: In monomeric ANGPTL4, Cys51 and Cys55 are connected by an intramolecular disulfide bond.
source: In monomeric ANGPTL4, we find that Cys51 and Cys55 are connected by an intramolecular disulfide bond, as demonstrated by masses of 3440.64 and 3442.64 Da for peptides corresponding to residues 45–77 in ANGPTL41–159 before and after reduction with tris-(2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C

claim: The catalytic activity of 1 µM ANGPTL41–159 is similar regardless of the integrity of the disulfide bond.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, the catalytic activity of 1 µM ANGPTL41–159 was similar regardless of the integrity of the disulfide bond.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D

claim: A covalent oligomer of ANGPTL41–159 is not essential for its catalytic LPL-unfolding activity in vitro.
source: In conclusion, a covalent oligomer of ANGPTL41–159 is not essential for its catalytic LPL-unfolding activity in vitro.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data comparing reduced/alkylated and native ANGPTL4

claim: In the absence of GPIHBP1, 87 ± 2% unfolding of LPL was observed after 10 min incubation with 2 µM ANGPTL41–159.
source: In the absence of GPIHBP1, we observed 87 ± 2% unfolding of LPL versus only 8 ± 2% unfolding in the presence of GPIHBP11–131 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: In the presence of GPIHBP11–131, only 8 ± 2% unfolding of LPL was observed after 10 min incubation with 2 µM ANGPTL41–159.
source: In the absence of GPIHBP1, we observed 87 ± 2% unfolding of LPL versus only 8 ± 2% unfolding in the presence of GPIHBP11–131 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 30 µM GPIHBP134–131 does not substantially inhibit ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding of LPL (79 ± 7% unfolding).
source: Both the LU domain and the acidic domain of GPIHBP1 (Figure 2C) were required for protecting LPL against ANGPTL4; neither 30 µM GPIHBP134–131 nor 30 µM GPIHBP11–33 substantially inhibited ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding of LPL (79 ± 7% and 69 ± 12% unfolding, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: 30 µM GPIHBP11–33 does not substantially inhibit ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding of LPL (69 ± 12% unfolding).
source: Both the LU domain and the acidic domain of GPIHBP1 (Figure 2C) were required for protecting LPL against ANGPTL4; neither 30 µM GPIHBP134–131 nor 30 µM GPIHBP11–33 substantially inhibited ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding of LPL (79 ± 7% and 69 ± 12% unfolding, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: The acidic domain of GPIHBP1 (GPIHBP11–33) is nearly as effective as full-length GPIHBP11–131 in protecting LPL from spontaneous unfolding.
source: A slightly different scenario emerged for spontaneous unfolding of LPL; the acidic domain of GPIHBP1 (GPIHBP11–33) was nearly as effective as full-length GPIHBP11–131 in protecting LPL from unfolding (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The GPIHBP11–33/GPIHBP134–131 mixture is less effective than full-length GPIHBP1 in protecting LPL from ANGPTL4-mediated unfolding.
source: The GPIHBP11–33/GPIHBP134–131 mixture was less effective than full-length GPIHBP1 in protecting LPL from ANGPTL4-mediated unfolding (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: GPIHBP1´s acidic domain needs to be tethered to the LU domain to achieve GPIHBP1´s full protective effect against ANGPTL4-catalyzed LPL unfolding.
source: In conclusion, it would appear that GPIHBP1´s acidic domain needs to be tethered to the LU domain to achieve GPIHBP1´s full protective effect against ANGPTL4-catalyzed LPL unfolding (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data comparing full-length GPIHBP1 with domain mixtures

claim: A covalent association of the two GPIHBP1 domains is less important for reducing the spontaneous unfolding of LPL.
source: A covalent association of the two GPIHBP1 domains is less important for reducing the spontaneous unfolding of LPL (Figure 2B).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The protection provided by different GPIHBP1 proteins against ANGPTL4-mediated LPL unfolding is accompanied by preserved LPL catalytic activity towards [3H]triolein substrate hydrolysis.
source: The protection provided by the different GPIHBP1 proteins against ANGPTL4-mediated LPL unfolding was accompanied by preserved LPL catalytic activity towards [3H]triolein substrate hydrolysis (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Adding GPIHBP1 to partially inactivated LPL protects the remaining LPL from inactivation.
source: As shown in Figure 3, adding GPIHBP1 to the partially inactivated LPL protected the remaining LPL from inactivation, but neither the spontaneously inactivated LPL nor the ANGPTL4-inactivated LPL was resurrected by GPIHBP1.
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 3

claim: Neither spontaneously inactivated LPL nor ANGPTL4-inactivated LPL is resurrected by GPIHBP1.
source: As shown in Figure 3, adding GPIHBP1 to the partially inactivated LPL protected the remaining LPL from inactivation, but neither the spontaneously inactivated LPL nor the ANGPTL4-inactivated LPL was resurrected by GPIHBP1.
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 3

claim: ANGPTL4 catalyzes LPL unfolding/inactivation in an irreversible manner.
source: Our studies further substantiates that ANGPTL4 catalyzes LPL unfolding/inactivation in an irreversible manner rather than acting as a noncompetitive and reversible inhibitor as previously suggested (Lafferty et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing no resurrection of inactivated LPL by GPIHBP1

claim: The ANGPTL4 variant ANGPTL4E15K results in the unfolding of 0.6 ± 0.1 molecules LPL per ANGPTL4 molecule per min.
source: The ANGPTL4 variant resulted in the unfolding of 0.6 ± 0.1 molecules LPL per ANGPTL4 molecule per min (Figure 4B and C), which is only 40% of the activity of wild-type ANGPTL4 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: ANGPTL4E15K has only 40% of the unfolding activity of wild-type ANGPTL4.
source: The ANGPTL4 variant resulted in the unfolding of 0.6 ± 0.1 molecules LPL per ANGPTL4 molecule per min (Figure 4B and C), which is only 40% of the activity of wild-type ANGPTL4 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: LPL incubated with ANGPTL41–159/E15K retained 40–50% more catalytic activity than LPL incubated with wild-type ANGPTL4.
source: We obtained consistent results when measuring LPL activity; the LPL incubated with ANGPTL41–159/E15K retained 40–50% more catalytic activity than LPL incubated with wild-type ANGPTL4 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 4D

claim: ANGPTL41–159/E15K loses activity more rapidly than wild-type ANGPTL4 during LPL incubation.
source: The LPL unfolding curves (Figure 4A and B) suggested that ANGPTL41–159/E15K lost activity more rapidly than wild-type ANGPTL4 during the LPL incubation.
evidence: Inference based on kinetic data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: Wild-type ANGPTL41–159 contains two regions that are less dynamic (residues 19–43 and 85–111).
source: As illustrated by the heat maps for deuterium uptake, wild-type ANGPTL41–159 contains two regions that are less dynamic (residues 19–43 and 85–111).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data

claim: Both less dynamic regions in ANGPTL4 (residues 19–43 and 85–111) are predicted by PSIPRED to form α-helices.
source: Both sequences are predicted by PSIPRED to form α-helices (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by PSIPRED prediction shown in Figure 5A

claim: The N-terminal α-helix of ANGPTL4 is less stable than the C-terminal α-helix.
source: Of the two α-helices, the N-terminal α-helix of ANGPTL4 is less stable (i.e., has a greater deuterium uptake).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data showing greater deuterium uptake

claim: The deuterium uptake in the N-terminal α-helix region of ANGPTL4 occurs via mixed EX1 and EX2 kinetics signifying some degree of cooperative unfolding.
source: The isotope envelopes reveal that the deuterium uptake in this particular region occurs via mixed EX1 and EX2 kinetics signifying some degree of cooperative unfolding (Weis et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data and citation to Weis et al., 2006

claim: Peptides covering residues 19–43 in ANGPTL41–159/E15K exchange more rapidly than in wild-type ANGPTL4.
source: A comparison of the kinetics for deuterium uptake into ANGPTL41–159/E15K and ANGPTL41–159/wt revealed a conspicuous difference: peptides covering residues 19–43 exchanged more rapidly in ANGPTL41–159/E15K (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5A and C

claim: The increased deuterium incorporation in ANGPTL4 E15K occurs predominantly via faster EX1 kinetics reflecting an increased propensity for cooperative unfolding.
source: The increased deuterium incorporation occurs predominantly via faster EX1 kinetics reflecting an increased propensity for cooperative unfolding of that region.
evidence: Supported by HDX-MS data analysis

claim: The Glu-to-Lys substitution in the E15K variant compromises protein stability by reducing the α-helix propensity of the adjacent C-terminal sequence.
source: Given that this region coincides with the predicted N-terminal α-helix in ANGPTL4, it is conceivable that the Glu-to-Lys substitution in the E15K variant compromises protein stability by reducing the α-helix propensity of the adjacent C-terminal sequence.
evidence: Speculation based on HDX-MS data and structural predictions

claim: ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4, and ANGPTL8 show strong sequence conservation in the N-terminal region that is destabilized in ANGPTL4E15K.
source: Sequence alignments of the different ANGPTL proteins implicated in triglyceride metabolism (ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4, ANGPTL8) reveal strong sequence conservation in the N-terminal region that is destabilized in ANGPTL4E15K (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6A

claim: ANGPTL3 accelerates the unfolding of the catalytic triad peptide leading to inactivation of LPL, but at reduced efficacy compared with equimolar amounts of ANGPTL4.
source: We found that ANGPTL3 also accelerates the unfolding of the catalytic triad peptide leading to inactivation of LPL, but at reduced efficacy compared with equimolar amounts of ANGPTL4 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: ANGPTL3-catalyzed inactivation of LPL is abrogated by GPIHBP1.
source: The ANGPTL3-catalyzed inactivation of LPL is abrogated by GPIHBP1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: GPIHBP1-bound LPL is protected from ANGPTL4 in vivo.
source: One implication of our findings is that only GPIHBP1-bound LPL would be protected from ANGPTL4 in vivo.
evidence: Inference based on in vitro experimental findings

claim: In the secretory pathway of adipocytes, where GPIHBP1 is absent, LPL would be more susceptible to ANGPTL4-mediated unfolding.
source: First, in the secretory pathway of adipocytes, where GPIHBP1 is absent, we suspect that LPL would be more susceptible to ANGPTL4-mediated unfolding.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings and knowledge of GPIHBP1 expression

claim: ANGPTL4 interacts with LPL in the trans-Golgi network, targeting it for lysosomal degradation.
source: Accordingly, recent studies of LPL production by mouse primary adipocytes and white adipose tissue explants indicate that ANGPTL4 interacts with LPL in the trans-Golgi network, targeting it for lysosomal degradation (Dijk et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dijk et al., 2016

claim: The endoplasmic reticulum has an efficient quality control system that targets thermodynamically unstable proteins for disposal via ERAD.
source: The endoplasmic reticulum has an efficient quality control system that targets thermodynamically unstable proteins for disposal via ERAD (Ellgaard and Helenius, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ellgaard and Helenius, 2003

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the trafficking receptor Vps10p serves as a protein-folding sensor diverting misfolded proteins to vacuolar disposal.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the trafficking receptor Vps10p serves as a protein-folding sensor diverting misfolded proteins to vacuolar disposal (Hong et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 1996

claim: SorLA is expressed by adipocytes and myocytes and targets newly synthesized LPL for degradation in lysosomes.
source: Interestingly, SorLA is also expressed by adipocytes and myocytes and targets newly synthesized LPL for degradation in lysosomes (Klinger et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klinger et al., 2011

claim: ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding of LPL in the trans-Golgi network may prime an anterograde sorting of SorLA-LPL complexes towards the endolysosomal degradation pathway.
source: One possibility—which obviously needs experimental testing—is that ANGPTL4-catalyzed unfolding of LPL in the trans-Golgi network primes an anterograde sorting of SorLA-LPL complexes towards the endolysosomal degradation pathway.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings and knowledge of protein quality control

claim: Angptl4-/- adipocytes secrete increased levels of LPL compared to wild-type adipocytes.
source: Such a mechanism might account for the increased LPL secretion from Angptl4-/- adipocytes compared to wild-type adipocytes (Dijk et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dijk et al., 2016

claim: Human adipocytes that express ANGPTL4 E15K polymorphism would secrete elevated levels of LPL.
source: In keeping with the latter idea, we speculate that human adipocytes that express ANGPTL4 E15K polymorphism would secrete elevated levels of LPL.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings about ANGPTL4 E15K reduced activity

claim: Freshly secreted LPL loosely associated with heparan-sulfate proteoglycans in the interstitial spaces is prone to inhibition by ANGPTL4.
source: Second, freshly secreted LPL—loosely associated with heparan-sulfate proteoglycans (HSPG) in the interstitial spaces—would also be prone to inhibition by ANGPTL4 (Olivecrona, 2016).
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings and citation to Olivecrona, 2016

claim: The interstitial space represents the primary target site for ANGPTL4-catalyzed inactivation of LPL.
source: It has been suggested that this compartment represents the primary target site for ANGPTL4-catalyzed inactivation of LPL (Nilsson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nilsson et al., 2012

claim: Translocation of LPL from the HSPG-bound reservoir to a GPIHBP1-bound state at the basolateral surface of endothelial cells alleviates the inhibitor repression exerted by ANGPTL4.
source: In this setting, translocation of LPL from the HSPG-bound reservoir to a GPIHBP1-bound state at the basolateral surface of endothelial cells would alleviate the inhibitor repression exerted by ANGPTL4.
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings about GPIHBP1 protection

claim: Inhibition of LPL within the interstitial spaces by locally produced ANGPTL4 is important for regulating the amount of active LPL that reaches the surface of capillaries.
source: We propose that inhibition of LPL within the interstitial spaces by locally produced ANGPTL4 is important for regulating the amount of active LPL that actually reaches the surface of capillaries, thereby serving to match the efficiency of intravascular lipolysis to the metabolic requirements of nearby parenchymal cells.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings and physiological reasoning

claim: The resistance of GPIHBP1-bound LPL to ANGPTL4- and ANGPTL3-mediated inhibition serves to focus catalytically active LPL at the luminal surface of capillary endothelial cells.
source: Finally, we propose that the resistance of GPIHBP1-bound LPL to ANGPTL4- and ANGPTL3-mediated inhibition serves to focus catalytically active LPL at the luminal surface of capillary endothelial cells.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings

claim: Human population studies have not uncovered a correlation between plasma ANGPTL4 levels and triglyceride concentrations.
source: It is interesting, that human population studies have not uncovered a correlation between plasma ANGPTL4 levels and triglyceride concentrations (Robciuc et al., 2010; Smart-Halajko et al., 2010) implying that the regulation of LPL activity in this compartment is far more convoluted.
evidence: Supported by citations to Robciuc et al., 2010 and Smart-Halajko et al., 2010

claim: Low-to-moderate concentrations of circulating ANGPTL4 and ANGPTL3 in the blood are insufficient to inhibit LPL in the presence of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins.
source: The low-to-moderate concentrations of circulating ANGPTL4 and ANGPTL3 in the blood are obviously insufficient to inhibit LPL in the presence of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (Nilsson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nilsson et al., 2012

claim: Elevated plasma levels of ANGPTL4 protein achieved by transgenic overexpression or systemic administration result in increased plasma triglyceride levels and vastly reduced post-heparin LPL activity levels in mice.
source: With that said, it is important to acknowledge that elevated plasma levels of ANGPTL4 protein achieved by transgenic overexpression or systemic administration clearly breached this protective barrier as these mice have increased plasma triglyceride levels and vastly reduced post-heparin LPL activity levels (Köster et al., 2005; Lichtenstein et al., 2007; Nilsson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies
